drugs.name: Ocrelizumab (Ocrevus)
drugs.mechanism: Humanized anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody; depletes CD20+ B cells via ADCC and CDC. B cell depletion reduces antigen presentation to T cells, pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and autoantibody secretion
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2017 (RMS and PPMS). First and only therapy approved for primary progressive MS.
drugs.efficacy: Reduces annualized relapse rate (ARR) by 46% vs IFNβ-1a in RMS; reduces confirmed disability progression by 24% in PPMS (ORATORIO). NEDA-3 achieved in ~48% at 2 years.

drugs.name: Ofatumumab (Kesimpta)
drugs.mechanism: Fully human anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody binding a distinct epitope from rituximab/ocrelizumab; depletes B cells via CDC and ADCC. Subcutaneous self-administration at home.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2020 (RMS). First self-administered B cell therapy for MS.
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 50-59% vs teriflunomide (ASCLEPIOS I/II). Superior to teriflunomide in reducing Gd+ lesions and disability progression.

drugs.name: Ublituximab (Briumvi)
drugs.mechanism: Glycoengineered chimeric anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody with enhanced ADCC; designed for rapid B cell depletion with shorter infusion times than rituximab
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2022 (RMS). First glycoengineered anti-CD20 for MS.
drugs.route: IV infusion: 1 hour (after first dose), every 6 months
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 49-59% vs teriflunomide (ULTIMATE I/II). Rapid B cell depletion within 24 hours. NEDA-3 achieved in ~44% at 96 weeks.

drugs.name: Rituximab (Rituxan)
drugs.mechanism: Chimeric anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody depleting B cells via ADCC, CDC, and apoptosis. Widely used off-label for MS in many countries.
drugs.approval: Used off-label for MS (not FDA-approved for MS). Strong real-world evidence from Swedish MS Registry.
drugs.efficacy: Observational studies show ARR reduction comparable to ocrelizumab. Superior to injectable DMTs in real-world Swedish data.

drugs.name: Natalizumab (Tysabri)
drugs.mechanism: Blocks α4β1 (VLA-4) and α4β7 integrins on lymphocytes, preventing their adhesion to VCAM-1 on blood-brain barrier endothelium → blocks lymphocyte migration into CNS
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2004 (RMS). Most effective non-B-cell-depleting DMT.
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 68% vs placebo (AFFIRM). PML risk: ~0.2-4.5 per 1,000 depending on JCV index, prior immunosuppressant use, and treatment duration.

drugs.name: Fingolimod (Gilenya)
drugs.mechanism: Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator; phosphorylated form binds S1PR1 on lymphocytes, causing receptor internalization → sequesters lymphocytes in lymph nodes, preventing egress into blood and CNS
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2010 (RMS). First oral DMT for MS.
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 54% vs placebo (FREEDOMS); 52% vs IFNβ-1a IM (TRANSFORMS). Reduces brain volume loss by ~35%.

drugs.name: Siponimod (Mayzent)
drugs.mechanism: Selective S1P1/S1P5 receptor modulator; S1P1 internalization sequesters lymphocytes in lymph nodes. S1P5 modulation on oligodendrocytes may promote remyelination. CNS-penetrant.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2019 (active SPMS, RMS). First oral therapy proven effective for active SPMS.
drugs.route: Oral, once daily (genotype-guided dosing for CYP2C9)
drugs.efficacy: Reduces 3-month confirmed disability progression by 21% in SPMS (EXPAND). Reduces ARR by 55% in RMS.

drugs.name: Ozanimod (Zeposia)
drugs.mechanism: Selective S1P1/S1P5 receptor modulator with no S1P3 activity (low cardiac risk: no first-dose bradycardia requiring monitoring). CNS-penetrant with potential remyelination effects via S1P5.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2020 (RMS). Also approved for ulcerative colitis (cross-disease S1P modulator).
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 48% vs IFNβ-1a (SUNBEAM); 38% vs IFNβ-1a (RADIANCE). Lower ARR and fewer Gd+ lesions than IFNβ-1a.

drugs.name: Ponesimod (Ponvory)
drugs.mechanism: Highly selective S1P1 receptor modulator with rapid receptor internalization kinetics. Short half-life (33 hours) allows rapid lymphocyte recovery within 1 week of discontinuation.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2021 (RMS). Superiority trial winner vs teriflunomide.
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 30.5% vs teriflunomide (OPTIMUM). Reduced fatigue symptoms vs teriflunomide. Rapid lymphocyte recovery upon discontinuation.

drugs.name: Dimethyl Fumarate (Tecfidera)
drugs.mechanism: Activates NRF2 antioxidant response pathway → anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects. Also agonizes HCAR2 (GPR109A) on immune cells. Metabolized to monomethyl fumarate.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2013 (RMS). Most prescribed oral DMT globally at its peak.
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 44-53% vs placebo (DEFINE/CONFIRM). Reduces disability progression by 38% vs placebo.

drugs.name: Diroximel Fumarate (Vumerity)
drugs.mechanism: Next-generation oral fumarate with improved GI tolerability. Prodrug converted to monomethyl fumarate (same active metabolite as dimethyl fumarate) with lower GI irritation.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2019 (RMS). Designed for better GI tolerability than dimethyl fumarate.
drugs.efficacy: Bioequivalent to dimethyl fumarate. EVOLVE-MS-2: significantly fewer days with GI side effects vs dimethyl fumarate (P < 0.0001).

drugs.name: Teriflunomide (Aubagio)
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits DHODH, blocking de novo pyrimidine synthesis → selectively reduces proliferation of activated T and B lymphocytes without killing resting cells
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2012 (RMS). First-line oral DMT.
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 31% vs placebo (TEMSO). Reduces disability progression by 30%. Often used as comparator arm in superiority trials of newer DMTs.

drugs.name: Cladribine (Mavenclad)
drugs.mechanism: Purine nucleoside analogue resistant to adenosine deaminase; accumulates in lymphocytes → DNA strand breaks → selective lymphocyte depletion (especially CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, B cells). Immune reconstitution therapy.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2019 (RMS, active SPMS). Short-course oral IRT.
drugs.route: Oral: 2 short courses (Year 1: 2 cycles; Year 2: 2 cycles), then possibly no further treatment for years
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 58% vs placebo (CLARITY). NEDA-3 achieved in 47% at 2 years. Durable effect: ~50% remain relapse-free at 4 years after last dose.

drugs.name: Alemtuzumab (Lemtrada)
drugs.mechanism: Depletes CD52+ T and B lymphocytes, monocytes, and NK cells via ADCC and CDC. Profound lymphocyte depletion followed by homeostatic reconstitution with altered immune repertoire (immune reset).
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2014 (RMS). Restricted use due to serious safety concerns (secondary autoimmunity ~30-40%, ITP, nephropathies, thyroid).
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 55% vs IFNβ-1a SC (CARE-MS I); 49% (CARE-MS II). 5-year follow-up: ~60% remain free of 6-month confirmed disability worsening.

drugs.name: Glatiramer Acetate (Copaxone)
drugs.target: MHC Class II / T Cell Repertoire
drugs.mechanism: Random copolymer of L-alanine, L-lysine, L-glutamic acid, L-tyrosine mimicking myelin basic protein (MBP). Competes for MHC class II binding; drives Th2 shift from Th1 in myelin-reactive T cells; promotes BDNF-producing neuroprotective T cells.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 1996 (RMS). Longest safety record among MS therapies.
drugs.route: Subcutaneous injection: daily (20 mg) or 3× weekly (40 mg)
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 29% vs placebo. Modest efficacy compared to modern DMTs but excellent safety profile.

drugs.name: Interferon Beta-1a / Beta-1b (Avonex, Rebif, Betaseron, Plegridy)
drugs.mechanism: Binds type I IFN receptor (IFNAR1/IFNAR2), activating JAK1/TYK2-STAT1/2 signaling. Reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines, inhibits T cell activation, reduces MMPs, and restores blood-brain barrier integrity
drugs.approval: FDA approved 1993-2014 (RMS, CIS). First DMT class for MS. Multiple formulations with different dosing frequencies.
drugs.route: Intramuscular (weekly) or subcutaneous (3× weekly, every 2 weeks PEGylated)
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 18-34% vs placebo. PEGylated IFN β-1a (Plegridy): ARR reduction 36% vs placebo. Modest efficacy but extensive long-term safety data.

drugs.name: Evobrutinib (Investigational)
drugs.mechanism: Highly selective, covalent BTK inhibitor. Inhibits BCR signaling in B cells and FcεR/FcγR signaling in myeloid cells (microglia, macrophages). CNS-penetrant — targets both peripheral and CNS-compartmentalized inflammation.
drugs.approval: Phase 3 (EVOLUTION RMS-1/2). Phase 2 met primary endpoint.
drugs.efficacy: Phase 2: reduced cumulative Gd+ lesions by 70-80% at 24 weeks. BTK inhibition addresses both peripheral B cells AND CNS-resident microglia — a unique dual mechanism.

drugs.name: Tolebrutinib (Investigational)
drugs.mechanism: CNS-penetrant, covalent BTK inhibitor with high CNS exposure. Designed to target smoldering MS pathology: inhibits microglial activation and B cell signaling within the CNS.
drugs.approval: Phase 3 (GEMINI-1/2 in RMS, HERCULES in progressive MS). FDA placed partial clinical hold (2022) due to liver injury cases; resumed with enhanced monitoring.
drugs.efficacy: Phase 2b: reduced Gd+ lesions by 85% at 12 weeks at 60 mg dose. Designed to address both relapsing biology and smoldering progression.

drugs.name: Mitoxantrone (Novantrone)
drugs.mechanism: Chemotherapeutic agent that intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, causing DNA strand breaks and cell death. Broad immunosuppression including B cells, T cells, and macrophages.
drugs.approval: FDA approved 2000 (worsening RMS, SPMS). Last-line therapy due to cardiotoxicity and leukemia risk. Strict 140 mg/m² lifetime cumulative dose limit.
drugs.efficacy: Reduces ARR by 60-70% and disability progression in active SPMS. Limited to 2-3 years of treatment due to cumulative cardiotoxicity.

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone (Solu-Medrol)
drugs.mechanism: High-dose IV corticosteroid for acute MS relapses. Rapidly reduces inflammation, restores BBB integrity, accelerates relapse recovery. No effect on long-term disease course or disability progression.
drugs.approval: Standard of care for acute MS relapses. Not a disease-modifying therapy.
drugs.route: IV: 1000 mg/day for 3-5 days (with or without oral taper)
drugs.efficacy: Accelerates recovery from acute relapses by ~3 weeks. Does not reduce long-term disability accumulation.
